correctness.rationale: Coercivity on the finite-dimensional candidate space gives existence; strict convexity and injectivity give uniqueness for each 1<p<infinity over complex coefficients. Conjugating coefficients and taking the (m+1)-reciprocal conjugate of the residual both preserve its norm. The second transformation sends (a,b) to (1+conj(b),conj(a)-1), using (1-z)f_m=1-z^(m+1); their fixed-point restrictions give real b=a-1. Then the residual has endpoints e=(1+t)/2 and m interior coefficients t. Parseval plus the finite correlation sums gives exactly the claimed quartic, and F_m'(-1)<0<F_m'(0) locates its unique minimum in (-1,0), proving the zero is real and >1. With u=-mt the rescaled objective m(F_m(-u/m)-3/8) and its first derivative equal Q(u) and Q'(u) up to O(1/m) on compact u intervals. Since Q''(u)=8u^2-12u+6>0 and Q'(0)<0<Q'(1), derivative signs at fixed bracketing points trap the global minimizers and give u_m=c+O(1/m) by the mean value theorem. Substitution proves the two sharp expansions, with positive kappa=-Q(c).
residual_risks: Finite exact tests do not prove the general quartic or asymptotics; universality rests on the scalar reduction and proof. Only the symmetry is claimed for every p.

value.rationale: The geometric sums give a natural degree-one approximation test as the boundary zeros of the generator change with length. The result explicitly measures the difference from Hilbert-space optimization in the first nonlinear even norm: the optimized zero displacement is about 0.715/m rather than 1/m, and the sharp first error correction is also determined. The scalar symmetry exposes why complex minimization does not require an extra complex search; the exact correction is more than a norm-comparison bound or numerical trend.
residual_risks: The calculation is not a classification for arbitrary generators, higher approximant degrees or growing p.
